L1543@P40: 4.7.1 \pdfpagesattr
L1544@P40: \pdfpagesattr (tokens)
L1545@P40: pdfTEX expands this token list when it finishes the PDF output and adds the resulting character
L1546@P40: stream to the root Pages object. When defined, these are applied to all pages in the document.

L1548@P40: displayed and printed, and /Rotate, the number of degrees (in multiples of 90) the page should be

L1553@P40: 4.7.2 \pdfpageattr
L1554@P40: \pdfpageattr (tokens)
L1555@P40: This is similar to \pdfpagesattr, but has priority over it. It can be used to override any
L1556@P40: attribute given by \pdfpagesattr for an individual page. The token list is expanded when pdfTEX
L1557@P40: ships out a page. The contents are added to the attributes of the current page.
L1558@P40: If the \pdfpageattr value contains the string /MediaBox, then pdfTEX omits outputting its own
L1559@P40: /MediaBox value (which is [0 0 ⟨page_width⟩ ⟨page_height⟩]). (This behavior was introduced in
L1560@P40: version 1.40.18.)

L1581@P41: 4.8 Form XObjects
L1582@P41: The next three primitives support a PDF feature called “object reuse” in pdfTEX. The idea is first to
L1583@P41: create a ‘form XObject’. The content of this object corresponds to the content of a TEX box; it can
L1584@P41: contain pictures and references to other form XObjects as well. After creation, the form XObject
L1585@P41: can be used multiple times by simply referring to its object number. This feature can be useful for
L1586@P41: large documents with many similar elements, to reduce the duplication of identical objects.
L1587@P41: These commands behave similarly to \pdfobj, \pdfrefobj and \pdflastobj (described in the
L1588@P41: previous section), but instead of taking raw PDF code, they handle text typeset by TEX.
L1589@P41: 4.8.1 \pdfxform

L1592@P41: ⟨resources spec⟩ → resources ⟨general text⟩

L1069@P28: \pdffontexpand). By default, \pdfadjustspacing is set to 0; then font expansion is disabled, so
L1070@P28: that the pdfTEX output is identical to that from the original TEX engine.
L1071@P28: Font expansion can be activated in two modes. When \pdfadjustspacing is set to 1, font
L1072@P28: expansion is applied after TEX’s normal paragraph breaking routines have broken the paragraph
L1073@P28: into lines. In this case, line breaks are identical to standard TEX behavior.
L1074@P28: When set to 2, the width changes that are the result of stretching and shrinking are taken into
L1075@P28: account while the paragraph is broken into lines. In this case, line breaks are likely to be different
L1076@P28: from those of standard TEX. Paragraphs may well become longer or shorter.
L1077@P28: Both alternatives require a collection of TFM files that are related to the ⟨stretch⟩ and ⟨shrink⟩
L1078@P28: settings for the \pdffontexpand primitive, unless this is given with the autoexpand option.
L1079@P28: 4.3.2 \pdffontexpand
L1080@P28: \pdffontexpand ⟨font⟩ ⟨stretch⟩ ⟨shrink⟩ ⟨step⟩ [ autoexpand ]
L1081@P28: This extension to TEX’s font definitions controls a major pdfTEX feature called font expansion.
L1082@P28: To enable font expansion, \pdfadjustspacing must be set to a value greater than zero. We describe
L1083@P28: the basic process with an example:
L1084@P28: \font\somefont=sometfm at 10pt
L1085@P28: \pdffontexpand\somefont 30 20 10 autoexpand
L1086@P28: \pdfadjustspacing=2
L1087@P28: The 30 20 10 means this: “hey TEX, when line breaking is going badly, you may stretch the
L1088@P28: glyphs from this font as much as 3% or shrink them as much as 2%.” For practical reasons pdfTEX
L1089@P28: uses discrete expansion steps, in this example, 1%.
L1090@P28: Roughly speaking, the idea is as follows: When TEX cannot break a line in the appropriate way,
L1091@P28: the unbreakable parts of the last word may stick into the margin. When pdfTEX sees this, it will
L1092@P28: try to scale (shrink) the glyphs in that line using fixed steps, until the line fits. When lines are too
L1093@P28: spacey, the opposite happens: pdfTEX starts scaling (stretching) the glyphs until the white space
L1094@P28: gaps are acceptable. This glyph stretching and shrinking is called font expansion.
L1095@P28: There are two different modes for font expansion, depending on whether autoexpand is specified:
L1096@P28: 1. If the autoexpand keyword is given—this is recommended mode—only a single map entry
L1097@P28: is needed for all expanded font versions, using the name of the unexpanded TFM file
L1098@P28: (tfmname in section 3.1.1). No expanded tfmname versions need be mentioned (indeed,
L1099@P28: they are ignored), as pdfTEX generates expanded instances of the unexpanded TFM data
L1100@P28: structures and keeps them in its memory. As of pdfTEX 1.40.0, the autoexpand work is
L1101@P28: done within the page stream by modification of the text matrix (PDF operator “Tm”), and
L1102@P28: not at the font file level, giving the advantage that it now works not only with Type 1
L1103@P28: but also with TrueType and OpenType fonts (and even without embedding a font file; but
L1104@P28: that’s not recommended). In this mode pdfTEX requires only unexpanded font files.
L1105@P28: 2. Second, if the autoexpand keyword is not given, setting up font expansion requires considerably more work, as there must be map entries for TFM files in all required expansion
L1106@P28: values. The expanded tfmname variants are constructed by adding the font expansion
L1107@P28-29: 29value to the tfmname of the base font, e.g., there must be a map entry with tfmname
L1108@P29: sometfm+10 for 1% stretch or sometfm-15 for 1.5% shrink. This also means that for each
L1109@P29: expanded font variant a TFM file with properly expanded metrics must exist. In addition
L1110@P29: to the TFM file, it is necessary to provide, for each expansion value, an individually crafted
L1111@P29: font file with the expanded glyphs. Thus, this allows the absolute best possible output,
L1112@P29: controlling the glyphs for every expanded variant of the font. It is a rare document indeed
L1113@P29: for this to be worth the trouble.
L1114@P29: One technical drawback of non-autoexpand mode is that all needed individual font files
L1115@P29: need to be embedded in the PDF output for each expanded font, leading to significantly
L1116@P29: larger PDF files than in autoexpand mode.
L1117@P29: Another caveat for non-autoexpand mode: when \pdffontexpand is executed, pdfTEX
L1118@P29: immediately loads two fonts, at the maximum stretch and shrink; in our example, sometfm+
L1119@P29: 30 and sometfm-20. (If they aren’t available, mktextfm may be uselessly called, and then
L1120@P29: an error message issued.) This happens even if those fonts never end up being used, which
L1121@P29: is arguably undesirable, but hard to change. It is not a problem when using autoexpand.
L1122@P29: The font expansion mechanism is inspired by an optimization first introduced by Prof. Hermann
L1123@P29: Zapf, which in itself goes back to optimizations used in the early days of typesetting: use different
L1124@P29: glyphs to optimize the grayness of a page. So, there are many, slightly different a’s, e’s, etc. For
L1125@P29: practical reasons pdfTEX does not use such huge glyph collections; it uses horizontal scaling instead.
L1126@P29: This is sub-optimal, and possibly offensive to the design, though the expansions are tiny. It is up
L1127@P29: to the user to decide whether such slightly remastered fonts are acceptable. As an example, this
L1128@P29: document is typeset with font expansion and margin kerning activated (via the microtype LATEX
L1129@P29: package).
L1130@P29: 4.3.3 \efcode
L1131@P29: \efcode ⟨font⟩ ⟨8-bit number⟩ (integer)
L1132@P29: We haven’t yet told the whole story. One can imagine that some glyphs are visually more
L1133@P29: sensitive to stretching or shrinking than others. Then the \efcode primitive can be used to influence
L1134@P29: the expandability of individual glyphs within a given font, as a factor applied to the expansion
L1135@P29: setting from the \pdffontexpand primitive. The syntax is similar to \sfcode (but with the ⟨font⟩
L1136@P29: required), and it defaults to 1000, meaning 100% expandability. The given integer value is clipped
L1137@P29: to the range 0..1000, corresponding to a usable expandability range of 0..100%. Examples:
L1138@P29: \efcode\somefont‘A=800
L1139@P29: \efcode\somefont‘O=0
L1140@P29: Here the A in \somefont may only stretch or shrink by up to 80% of the current expansion
L1141@P29: value for that font, and expansion for the O is disabled. The actual expansion is still bound to the
L1142@P29: steps as defined by \pdffontexpand primitive.
L1143@P29: Changes to this table are global, i.e., ignore TEX’s usual grouping, and apply only to the given
L1144@P29: ⟨font⟩.
L1145@P29: 4.3.4 \pdfprotrudechars
L1146@P29: \pdfprotrudechars (integer)
L1147@P29: Yet another way of optimizing paragraph breaking is to let certain characters move into the
L1148@P29: margin (‘character protrusion’). Character protrusion is disabled when \pdfprotrudechars=0 or
L1149@P29: negative.
L1150@P29-30: 30When \pdfprotrudechars=1, the glyphs qualified as such will make this move when applicable,
L1151@P30: without changing the line-breaking. When \pdfprotrudechars=2 (or greater), character protrusion
L1152@P30: will be taken into account while considering breakpoints, so line-breaking might be changed. This
L1153@P30: qualification and the amount of shift are set by the primitives \rpcode and \lpcode.

L2407@P62: 4.23.2 \tracinglostchars
L2408@P62: \tracinglostchars (integer)
L2409@P62: This primitive parameter has always been part of TEX, and its operation with values ≤ 2 is
L2410@P62: unchanged. In addition, if its value is ≥ 3, then “Missing character” reports become full errors
L2411@P62: (ordinarily they are only logged), and the character code is reported in hex. For example:
L2412@P62: \tracinglostchars=3
L2413@P62: \font\x=logo10 \x \char99 \end
L2414@P62-63: 63will result in this error message:
L2415@P63: ! Missing character: There is no c ("63) in font logo10.
L2416@P63: (The logo10 font only defines the capital letters used in the METAFONT and MetaPost logos, so
L2417@P63: there is no lowercase.)
L2418@P63: This new behavior is essentially the same in all TEX engines except the original TEX and ε-TEX,
L2419@P63: where the behavior of \tracinglostchars remains unchanged.
L2420@P63: The primitive was introduced in pdfTEX 1.40.22.
L2421@P63: 4.23.3 \tracingstacklevels
L2422@P63: \tracingstacklevels (integer)
L2423@P63: If this primitive parameter is > 0, and \tracingmacros > 0, macro expansion logging is truncated at the specified depth. Also, and more importantly, each relevant log line is given a prefix
L2424@P63: beginning with ~, either followed by a . character for each expansion level or another ~ if the
L2425@P63: expansion was truncated. For example:
L2426@P63: \tracingmacros=1 % so macro expansion is logged at all
L2427@P63: \tracingstacklevels=2 % cut off at level 2
L2428@P63: \def\a#1{\relax} % argument to show parameter logging is affected too
L2429@P63: \def\b#1{\a{#1}}
L2430@P63: \b1
L2431@P63: logs the following:
L2432@P63: ~.\b #1->\a {#1}
L2433@P63: #1<-1
L2434@P63: ~~\a
L2435@P63: Thus, the expansion of \b is logged normally, with the addition of the ~. prefix. The expansion
